name: Women’s Day
shortDescription: Lerato expects her Women’s Day homework to be boring, until Khanyisa opens a living journey into the women who resisted pass laws, organised the 1956 march and showed how unity can change history.
longDescription: After school, Lerato and Khanyisa head to their local library to complete a Women’s Day assignment. Lerato expects another piece of boring history, but Khanyisa begins telling the story and the pages of an old history book unfold into living memories. The girls witness how pass laws restricted where Black South Africans could live, work and travel; learn about women who resisted pass laws before 1956; see families separated by long journeys, checkpoints and arrests; and watch women organise across the country. Trains, buses, cars, bicycles, lorries and walking routes converge on Pretoria as thousands of women carry petitions to the Union Buildings. The story introduces the organisers of the 1956 Women’s March and builds toward the defining image of approximately twenty thousand women standing together in disciplined silence before their voices rise in song. Petition pages and signatures form a symbolic rock, representing collective strength. The history then flows into the present through the everyday work of teachers, nurses, scientists, judges, farmers, builders, artists, athletes, business owners, police officers, taxi drivers, cleaners, caregivers and community organisers. Back at the library, Lerato and Khanyisa create a display honouring both historical leaders and women in their own neighbourhood. At the unfinished end of the display they add their own names, recognising that history belongs to every generation and that the work of building dignity, safety and equality continues. The Panda Kids Club adaptation uses premium dimensional watercolour CGI for the present day and increasingly cinematic living-paper historical scenes built from petitions, pass documents, maps, signatures and painted footsteps.

attribution.author: Thelma Mhlari
attribution.adaptationNote: Adapted for animation by Panda Kids Club from the source title Women’s Day. The source story follows Lerato and Khanyisa as Khanyisa explains why 9 August is National Women’s Day, the apartheid pass system, earlier women’s resistance to passes, the 1956 Women’s March to the Union Buildings, the leaders associated with the march, the women’s disciplined silence and the continuing importance of women’s rights. The Panda Kids Club adaptation preserves this historical and civic foundation while expanding the story into a cinematic library-to-history journey. Changes include opening with a contemporary South African community beginning National Women’s Day; turning Lerato’s loose homework page into a recurring visual bridge into history; expanding the pass-law section through checkpoints, divided routes, delayed parents and symbolic paper barriers; introducing earlier resistance through a dignified 1913 sequence associated with Charlotte Maxeke; showing how women organised privately and travelled to Pretoria by train, bus, car, bicycle, lorry and foot; presenting Lillian Ngoyi, Helen Joseph, Rahima Moosa, Sophia Williams-De Bruyn and Bertha Gxowa as active organisers rather than static portraits; making the thirty minutes of silence at the Union Buildings the emotional centre of the film; using petition pages and signatures to form a symbolic rock representing collective strength; connecting the march to later generations of South African women working across many professions and community roles; and expanding the ending so Lerato and Khanyisa research women in their own neighbourhood, build a library display titled THE WOMEN WHO MAKE OUR COMMUNITY STRONG, and add their own names at the unfinished end of the procession. The adaptation intentionally avoids suggesting that equality has been completed and ends on the idea that courage, responsibility and the work of building safety, dignity and equality continue across generations. The visual adaptation uses premium stylised dimensional watercolour CGI inspired by handcrafted animated storybooks, with the contemporary library and neighbourhood rendered warmly and consistently while historical scenes grow from flat paper-and-charcoal illustrations into fully dimensional cinematic crowds. Petition pages, pass documents, maps, signatures, painted footsteps and the symbolic rock serve as recurring visual motifs.
